title: Blunt chest trauma: flail chest and pulmonary contusion

brief.role: Core surgical trainee in the trauma team
brief.scenario: Mr Faulkner, 67, was the driver in a side-impact car crash. He is alert and talking. Respiratory rate 30/min, SpO2 91% on 15 L/min oxygen by reservoir mask, pulse 104/min, BP 138/82 mmHg. Part of his left chest wall moves inwards when he breathes in.
brief.task: The airway and cervical spine have been assessed by the team leader. Discuss your assessment and management of his chest injury with the examiner.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Flail chest is a sign of a bad lung underneath. Treat the contusion and the pain.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Intubating because a flail is present, or sending him to the ward because gases look acceptable now.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "This is a flail segment. I'd first exclude tension pneumothorax and massive haemothorax."

grid.label: Recognises a flail segment
grid.fail: Calls it 'a broken rib' or does not recognise paradoxical movement.
grid.pass: Adjacent ribs each broken in two or more places, so a segment moves inwards on inspiration.
grid.high: Separates the clinical sign (paradox) from the radiological segment, and knows splinting from pain can hide paradox early.

grid.label: Excludes immediate threats
grid.fail: Focuses on the ribs without checking for tension pneumothorax or haemothorax.
grid.pass: Re-examines breathing: trachea, percussion, air entry. Chest X-ray or eFAST in the primary survey if respiratory compromise is severe.
grid.high: Decompresses before imaging only if haemodynamically unstable or in severe respiratory compromise; CT chest once he is stable or responding.

grid.label: Explains the hypoxia
grid.fail: Blames the hypoxia on the paradoxical movement alone.
grid.pass: Hypoxia comes mainly from the underlying pulmonary contusion, plus pain-limited breathing causing atelectasis and retained secretions.
grid.high: Expects the contusion to worsen over the next days, so acceptable early gases do not mean he is safe.

grid.label: Analgesia
grid.fail: Offers oral analgesia only, or withholds opioids 'to protect his breathing'.
grid.pass: Titrated IV morphine first, then early regional analgesia so he can breathe deeply and cough.
grid.high: Epidural preferred in severe flail chest; paravertebral block if epidural is contraindicated. Tracks pain scores and ability to cough.

grid.label: Ventilatory support and fluids
grid.fail: Intubates because a flail is present, or restricts fluids severely.
grid.pass: Oxygen and chest physiotherapy; trial of mask CPAP if alert with marginal respiratory status; intubates for respiratory failure, not for the flail.
grid.high: Resuscitates to adequate perfusion, then avoids unnecessary fluid; no steroids for the contusion.

grid.label: Surgical rib fixation
grid.fail: Says flail chest is always managed without surgery.
grid.pass: Surgical stabilisation of rib fractures should be considered in all patients with flail chest, ideally within 48 to 72 hours.
grid.high: Knows the benefits (less ventilation, pneumonia, tracheostomy, ICU stay and mortality) and that haemodynamic instability rules it out.

grid.label: Disposition and escalation
grid.fail: Admits him to a general ward on oral analgesia.
grid.pass: High dependency or critical care bed under a named trauma team, with serial blood gases and reassessment.
grid.high: Asks early for an anaesthetic regional block and a thoracic opinion on fixation; flags his age as raising risk.

fail.text: What is happening to his chest wall?

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: What is happening to his chest wall?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: This is a flail segment: adjacent ribs each broken in two or more places, so that segment moves inwards when he breathes in.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Re-examine his breathing: trachea, percussion, air entry, to exclude tension pneumothorax and haemothorax. With this degree of compromise, a chest X-ray or eFAST in the primary survey.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Mainly the pulmonary contusion underneath, plus pain stopping him breathing deeply, which leads to atelectasis and retained secretions.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: How will you manage his pain?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Titrated IV morphine now, then early regional analgesia so he can breathe deeply and cough.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Not for the flail itself. Oxygen and physiotherapy, and a trial of mask CPAP if he stays alert but marginal. I'd intubate if he goes into respiratory failure.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Is there any role for surgery?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Yes. Surgical rib fixation should be considered in flail chest, ideally within 48 to 72 hours.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: High dependency or critical care under the trauma team, with serial gases.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: What is happening to his chest wall?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: A flail chest: the clinical sign is paradoxical movement; the flail segment is the radiological finding of adjacent ribs each broken in two or more places. Pain splinting can hide the paradox early, so I'd look for it on CT too.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Exclude tension pneumothorax and massive haemothorax. He is haemodynamically stable, so I'd only decompress before imaging if he became unstable or his breathing got much worse. Once he is stable, CT chest.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: His first gas on 15 litres shows a PaO2 of 9 kPa. Reassured?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: No. The contusion is the main problem and it tends to get worse over the next days, so I'd expect his gas exchange to deteriorate before it improves.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: IV morphine titrated now, and I'd ask the anaesthetist for an epidural, which is preferred in severe flail chest, or a paravertebral catheter if an epidural isn't possible. I'd judge success by whether he can cough.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Resuscitate him to adequate perfusion, then avoid unnecessary fluid, because it worsens the contused lung. Steroids have no role.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I'd ask the thoracic team to consider it within 48 to 72 hours. Fixation reduces ventilator days, pneumonia, tracheostomy, ICU stay and mortality. It isn't done while he is haemodynamically unstable.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: At 67 with multiple rib fractures he is at higher risk, so I'd want critical care involved from the start, not after he tires.

failures.move: Intubating because a flail segment is present.
failures.consequence: Exposes him to ventilator-associated pneumonia when analgesia and CPAP may have avoided ventilation.

failures.move: Withholding opioids and regional analgesia to 'protect his breathing'.
failures.consequence: Pain stops him coughing and breathing deeply; atelectasis and pneumonia follow.

failures.move: Concentrating on the ribs before excluding tension pneumothorax or haemothorax.
failures.consequence: Misses the injury that can kill him in minutes.

failures.move: Admitting to a general ward because the first gas is acceptable.
failures.consequence: Contusion worsens over days; he deteriorates unwatched.

recovery.when: Asked whether he needs a tube
recovery.line: Not for the flail itself: I'd treat the pain and the lung, and intubate only for respiratory failure.
I'd go back to the primary survey and exclude tension pneumothorax and haemothorax first.

knowledge.fact: Flail chest is the clinical sign of paradox. WSES/CWIS define a radiological flail segment as three or more consecutive ribs each broken in two or more places.
Respiratory failure is driven mainly by the underlying contusion and by pain-limited breathing.
Epidural is the preferred analgesia in severe flail chest; paravertebral if epidural is contraindicated. Avoid ventilation without respiratory failure; consider mask CPAP.
Consider rib fixation in all flail chest, within 48 to 72 hours; not while haemodynamically unstable.
Consider CT chest for adults without severe respiratory compromise who are stable or responding to resuscitation.

recall.think: Hidden tension pneumothorax or haemothorax; contusion worsening over days.
recall.say: "Flail segment with underlying contusion: analgesia, not automatic intubation."
do: IV morphine, then epidural or paravertebral
Oxygen, physiotherapy, CPAP; critical care bed

partner.opening: This man has just arrived. Tell me what is happening to his chest wall and what worries you.

reveals.finding: Trachea central. Reduced air entry at the left base, resonant to percussion. Paradoxical segment left lateral chest wall.

reveals.trigger: Candidate asks for a chest X-ray or eFAST
reveals.finding: Left ribs 4 to 7 fractured anteriorly and posteriorly. Patchy left mid-zone opacification. No pneumothorax or haemothorax.

reveals.trigger: Candidate asks for a blood gas
reveals.finding: On 15 L/min: PaO2 9 kPa, PaCO2 5.8 kPa, lactate 1.4.
Pain 9/10; he cannot cough or take a deep breath.

push.question: Why is he hypoxic?
push.expect: Underlying contusion and pain-limited breathing, not the paradox itself.

push.question: How will you control his pain?
push.expect: IV morphine now; epidural preferred, paravertebral if not.

push.question: Should we intubate him now?
push.expect: No: CPAP trial if alert and marginal; intubate for respiratory failure.

push.question: Is there a role for surgery?
push.expect: Consider rib fixation in flail chest within 48–72 hours; not if unstable.

push.question: Where should he be managed?
push.expect: HDU or critical care under a named trauma team.

curveballs.prompt: His saturations are 96% after morphine. Can he go to the ward?
curveballs.safeAnswer: No. The contusion may worsen over the next days; critical care with serial gases.

curveballs.prompt: He suddenly becomes hypotensive and his trachea deviates to the right.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Left tension pneumothorax: immediate decompression, then chest drain.

curveballs.prompt: Should he have steroids for the lung contusion?
curveballs.safeAnswer: No. Steroids are not used for pulmonary contusion.

curveballs.prompt: He becomes hypotensive with distended neck veins; trachea central, air entry unchanged.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Consider cardiac tamponade: eFAST pericardial view and immediate senior and cardiothoracic help (see MB-261).
